text: Sort an integer array in ascending order — without using the built-in sort, ideally in n log n time or better.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Are the values bounded integers, and can they be negative? That decides whether I can beat the n log n comparison lower bound with a non-comparison sort like radix.
Values fit in thirty-two-bit ints and can be negative. Duplicates allowed.

Bounded integers — so radix sort gets me order d times n, effectively linear, beating the comparison bound. I'll need to handle negatives specially, since digit extraction assumes non-negative numbers.

Let me lay out the landscape. Comparison sorts bottom out at n log n — that's a proven lower bound, since telling apart n factorial permutations needs a decision tree of depth log of n factorial, which is n log n. Merge sort is stable with that worst case but needs linear extra space; heap sort is in-place with the same guarantee; quicksort is fastest on average but quadratic in the worst case. This problem reminds me of non-comparison sorting: when keys are bounded integers, digits can be used directly as array indices. So I'll go with LSD radix sort, which sidesteps the bound entirely.

Here's the plan. One: split the array into non-negatives and negatives, storing the negatives as absolute values. Two: for each digit, ones, tens, hundreds, run a stable counting sort on that digit. Three: reverse the sorted negatives, negate them, and put them in front of the positives. Two things worth flagging. First, each digit pass must be a stable counting sort — I fill from right to left with a prefix sum, so equal digits keep their order; otherwise a higher digit would scramble the lower-digit work. Second, negatives: I reverse them because the largest magnitude is the most negative. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code the radix version.

Let me write it. The radix helper is a counting sort on one digit: count each digit, turn the counts into end positions with a prefix sum, then place elements. Radix sort splits by sign, runs that helper digit by digit on both halves, then reverses and negates the negatives and puts them first. Sort array just calls radix sort and returns the array. One detail worth flagging — the placement loop runs from back to front, decrementing the count before writing. With prefix-sum end positions, that's exactly what makes each digit pass stable. Run it front to back and equal digits come out reversed, which breaks the earlier passes.

Let's dry-run negative five, fifty-three, negative eight, twenty-four, six — expected negative eight, negative five, six, twenty-four, fifty-three. The positives sort normally, digit by digit. The row that matters is the negatives: stored as five and eight, reversed to eight, five, then negated to negative eight, negative five — so the most negative leads. Combined, that matches. Corner cases: an empty array, where the loops just skip; all equal values, where stability keeps the order; and a single zero. All of them check out against the standard sort on thirty thousand random arrays with negatives and duplicates.

Time is order d times n, where d is the digit count — effectively linear for thirty-two-bit ints, since d is at most ten. Space is linear for the counting buffers. It beats the comparison lower bound because it never compares two elements — digits index directly. One more thing — if values were unbounded or not integers, radix wouldn't apply, and I'd fall back to merge sort, which is stable, or heap sort, which is in-place and safe in the worst case. A general-purpose choice would be introsort, which is what the standard library sort uses.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: scoping the input to justify a non-comparison sort, the stability argument for per-digit counting, and the negative-number trick of split, reverse, negate — plus knowing the comparison fallbacks. Good work.
